title: Cofactr vs. Supplyframe: What Changed for Electronics Buyers After the Siemens Acquisition
summary: Siemens bought Supplyframe in 2021. What changed for Findchips & SamacSys users, Siemens EDA teams, and where Cofactr fits in supply chain execution.
body_markdown:
##


When Siemens acquired Supplyframe in 2021, it acquired much more than a software application. It acquired access to a large-scale source of electronics intelligence generated by the interactions of engineers, buyers, and supply-chain professionals across the industry.


Supplyframe's strategic value was not only its software products. It was the information generated through its ecosystem: component searches, design resources, supply-chain activity, demand signals, and risk signals.


We'll look at what the acquisition changed for three groups: existing Supplyframe enterprise customers, Siemens EDA customers, and everyone else who uses Supplyframe's ecosystem, even if they don't realize it.


## What Is Supplyframe?


Supplyframe is easiest to understand as a collection of products aimed at different parts of the electronics industry, all built around component and supply-chain intelligence.


### DSI Solutions for Global Manufacturers


These are Supplyframe's SaaS products for OEMs, used by engineering, sourcing, and supply-chain teams. They include:


- Supplyframe NPI
- Supplyframe DirectSource


### DSI Solutions for Suppliers and Distributors


Supplyframe also sells products to semiconductor manufacturers, suppliers, and distributors. These include:


- Supplyframe Media Solutions
- Supplyframe DesignSense
- Supplyframe CPQ, which uses component intelligence to help semiconductor companies price and quote their products


### EMS Solutions


Supplyframe also has a group of products aimed at EMS companies, including:


- Buy Manager
- Win and Design Win
- Supplyframe XQ


### DSI Network Sites


Then there are Supplyframe's Network Sites, which are the part of the company many engineers and buyers encounter without ever becoming a Supplyframe enterprise customer. These are free, public-facing resources and include:


- Findchips
- SamacSys
- ComponentSearchEngine.com, the public-facing interface to SamacSys
- EEFocus
- OEMsTrade
- BOM2BOM


Those network sites are especially important to understanding why Siemens wanted Supplyframe. They attract engineers, buyers, and supply-chain professionals performing ordinary tasks such as searching for components, comparing availability, finding technical data, and downloading design resources. At scale, those interactions generate the design, demand, supply, and risk signals that feed Supplyframe's broader intelligence business.


That means Supplyframe is better understood as a portfolio with three broad layers: enterprise intelligence products for OEMs, commercial tools for suppliers and EMS companies, and a large public network that generates substantial electronics-industry activity.


## Why Supplyframe Is Different From Siemens' Other Acquisitions


After Siemens acquired Mentor Graphics in 2017, it expanded its EDA portfolio through additional acquisitions that generally followed a familiar pattern. The acquired technology became part of Siemens EDA, the original company identity faded, and the products were folded into Siemens' broader software portfolio.


OneSpin followed that pattern after Siemens acquired it in 2021, with its formal verification technology becoming part of the Siemens EDA verification portfolio. UltraSoC followed a similar path, becoming part of the Tessent ecosystem.


Supplyframe was treated differently.


Siemens acquired Supplyframe in 2021, but Supplyframe continues operating under its own name and with its own public-facing identity. More unusually, Siemens remains invisible across all of Supplyframe's public-facing properties. Findchips remains Findchips. SamacSys remains SamacSys. Component Search Engine remains Component Search Engine. Supplyframe's enterprise products also continue to be marketed under the Supplyframe name. Someone using those resources in the normal course of engineering work could easily have no idea they were interacting with a Siemens-owned business.


Siemens therefore acquired something unusual in its EDA history: an externally recognizable electronics intelligence ecosystem that continues to operate under its own brands while becoming part of Siemens' broader industrial software business.


## What Changed for Existing Supplyframe Customers?


If you were already using Supplyframe before Siemens acquired it, less changed than you might expect.


Supplyframe kept its name, its product names, its customer-facing identity, and its existing product categories. The company[told customers](https://intelligence.supplyframe.com/acquisition-questions-and-answers/) there would be no near-term changes to products, contracts, account contacts, or customer-success relationships.


That continuity is one of the most unusual parts of the acquisition. Existing Supplyframe customers were not pushed onto replacement Siemens products, and the Supplyframe brand remained intact.


For existing Supplyframe enterprise customers, the acquisition primarily expanded integration opportunities rather than changing how Supplyframe itself looked or operated.


## What Changed for Siemens EDA Customers?


The acquisition had a much bigger impact on Siemens EDA customers than it did on existing Supplyframe customers.


Before Siemens acquired Supplyframe, engineering teams and supply-chain teams often worked with different sets of information. Engineers selected components based on electrical and mechanical requirements. Procurement teams later evaluated availability, lifecycle risk, lead times, pricing, and alternate sources. Sometimes those two worlds align. Sometimes they collided after the design was already committed.


The acquisition gave Siemens an opportunity to move supply-chain intelligence much closer to the engineering process.


One of the first major examples[came in 2023](https://press.siemens.com/global/en/pressrelease/siemens-brings-real-time-supply-chain-intelligence-siemens-xcelerator-and-digital-twin) , when Siemens integrated Supplyframe's Design-to-Source Intelligence platform into Xpedition. Engineers could view availability, demand, cost, compliance, and parametric information while selecting components, allowing supply-chain considerations to become part of the design process instead of a separate activity performed later by procurement.


Siemens followed with a Teamcenter integration that allows BOMs to move into Supplyframe NPI for risk analysis, alternate recommendations, and RFQ workflows before returning that information to the PLM environment.


For organizations already using Siemens software, these integrations brought engineering and supply-chain data closer together. Component decisions could incorporate availability, lifecycle information, compliance, cost, alternate components, and broader supply-chain intelligence much earlier in the product-development process.


For Siemens EDA customers, the acquisition primarily extended the design environment into a more supply-aware workflow.


## What Changed for Everyone Else?


The largest group affected by the acquisition is probably people who never thought of themselves as Supplyframe customers in the first place.


You may use Findchips to check stock and pricing, or Component Search Engine to access SamacSys ECAD models such as symbols, footprints, and 3D models. You may also encounter EEFocus, OEMsTrade, or BOM2BOM without ever visiting Supplyframe's enterprise product pages.


Those tools continued to look familiar after the acquisition. Findchips remained Findchips. Component Search Engine remained the public-facing access point to the SamacSys design-resource dataset.


What changed was the ownership context.


The activity generated across those properties now sits inside a Siemens-owned ecosystem.[Supplyframe describes](https://intelligence.supplyframe.com/it/supplyframe-and-orbweaver-partner-accelerate-data-integration/) that ecosystem as involving more than 12 million engineering and supply-chain professionals generating billions of signals related to design intent, demand, supply, and risk.


Those signals are part of what makes Supplyframe valuable. Component searches, design-resource activity, sourcing behavior, and broader supply-chain interactions can all contribute to a larger picture of what is happening across the electronics industry.


So if you use one of Supplyframe's public network sites, the acquisition may not have changed your day-to-day experience very much. The more important change is that your activity now contributes to an electronics intelligence ecosystem owned by Siemens.


That raises a more interesting question than whether the logo changed: how Siemens uses the signals generated by engineers and buyers across Supplyframe's network as it continues integrating Supplyframe intelligence into its broader software portfolio.


## Why Cofactr Is a Different Answer to the Problem


Supplyframe and Cofactr overlap in a few obvious places. Both can help you evaluate BOMs, identify sourcing risk, look at availability, and find alternate components.


The difference is what each platform is primarily built to do.


Supplyframe is strongest as an intelligence and decision layer. Its products help engineering, sourcing, and supply-chain teams understand which parts are risky, constrained, expensive, approaching end of life, or otherwise likely to create problems before those parts become a production issue.


Cofactr is built much further downstream into execution. Once the component decision is made, Cofactr can handle sourcing, supplier coordination, purchasing, receiving, authentication, inventory, kitting, and delivery to production.


That distinction is especially important for lean hardware teams. Knowing that a part is available, risky, or overpriced is useful. Someone still has to place the order, manage the supplier, receive the material, track the inventory, and get the right parts to the right build.


A simple way to think about the difference is:


Supplyframe helps answer, "Are we making the right component decisions?"


Cofactr helps answer, "Can we reliably get those components into production?"


## How Electronics Buyers Should Evaluate Supplyframe vs. Cofactr


The easiest way to compare the two is to start with the problem your team is actually trying to solve.


If your biggest concern is integrating component intelligence directly into CAD and engineering workflows, especially if those tools are already in the Siemens ecosystem, Supplyframe deserves a close look. That includes environments built around Xpedition or PADS, where component data can sit much closer to the engineering decisions that determine what goes onto the BOM. Siemens has also connected Supplyframe intelligence with Teamcenter, extending that information into PLM workflows.


If your bigger problem begins after the BOM is approved, Cofactr is oriented around[supply chain execution](https://www.cofactr.com/products) . The platform carries component decisions into sourcing, supplier coordination, purchasing, receiving, authentication, inventory management, kitting, and delivery to production.


These tools are not mutually exclusive. There is some overlap in areas such as component intelligence, BOM analysis, sourcing, availability, and alternates, but they address different parts of the workflow. You could already be using Supplyframe to bring component intelligence into your design process and still get substantial value from Cofactr for supply chain execution.


A useful evaluation should therefore focus on where your team is spending time and where problems are escaping into the next stage of the process. Supplyframe can sit closer to component selection and design decisions. Cofactr can take an approved component decision and carry it through the operational work required to put physical material in front of production.


A good test uses your own BOMs rather than a generic product demo. Include difficult alternates, lifecycle issues, shortages, and sourcing problems your team has actually encountered. Then look at what each platform identifies, where it fits into your existing systems, and how much manual work remains between the software's recommendation and material arriving for the build.


## Closing Remark


Supplyframe was unusual because Siemens acquired an electronics intelligence ecosystem rather than another software product to fold into Siemens EDA.


The effect depends on where you sit. Existing Supplyframe customers mostly kept the products, brands, and customer experience they already knew, while gaining access to deeper Siemens integration. Siemens EDA customers gained a tighter connection between component intelligence and design or PLM workflows. Everyone else continued using familiar public resources such as Findchips and Component Search Engine, even though those resources now sit inside a Siemens-owned ecosystem.\[1-3\]


The larger lesson for electronics teams is that better component decisions and better supply chain execution are separate problems.


Supplyframe is built primarily to help you answer, "What should we build with?"


Cofactr is built to help you answer, "How do we reliably build it?"


Those jobs can overlap, and the tools can coexist. If Supplyframe already gives your engineers the component intelligence they need inside Xpedition, PADS, or another design workflow, that does not eliminate the purchasing, supplier coordination, inventory, authentication, kitting, and delivery work required to get those parts into production. That is where Cofactr's supply chain execution model fits.\[7-9\]

## Frequently Asked Questions


**What is Supplyframe?**


Supplyframe is an electronics intelligence portfolio covering OEMs, suppliers, distributors, and EMS companies, alongside public network sites including Findchips, SamacSys, Component Search Engine, EEFocus, and BOM2BOM.


**Why did Siemens acquire Supplyframe?**


Siemens acquired Supplyframe in 2021 for its electronics intelligence capabilities and extensive network activity, involving more than 12 million engineering and supply-chain professionals generating billions of industry signals.


**How did the Siemens acquisition affect existing Supplyframe customers?**


Existing customers saw limited immediate disruption. Supplyframe retained its company name, product names, customer-facing identity, contracts, account contacts, and customer-success relationships while gaining additional Siemens integration opportunities.


**How does Supplyframe integrate with Siemens EDA tools?**


Supplyframe intelligence integrates with Xpedition and Teamcenter, giving teams access to component availability, demand, cost, compliance, lifecycle information, alternates, risk analysis, and RFQ workflows during development.


**Can I use Findchips or SamacSys without being a Supplyframe enterprise customer?**


Yes. Findchips, SamacSys, Component Search Engine, EEFocus, OEMsTrade, and BOM2BOM are public network resources used for component searches, technical information, availability checks, and design resources.


**What is the main difference between Cofactr and Supplyframe?**


Supplyframe concentrates primarily on component intelligence and decision support. Cofactr extends into supply-chain execution, including sourcing, purchasing, supplier coordination, receiving, authentication, inventory, kitting, and production delivery.


**Is Cofactr an alternative to Supplyframe for electronics buyers?**


It can address different requirements. Supplyframe supports component selection and supply-chain intelligence, while Cofactr handles operational work required to source, receive, manage, kit, and deliver physical components.


**How should electronics teams compare Supplyframe and Cofactr?**


Test both platforms using real BOMs containing shortages, lifecycle problems, difficult alternates, and sourcing issues. Compare identified risks, system integrations, workflow coverage, and remaining manual work before production.
